title: Treating Burns
summary: How to treat thermal burns safely without medical equipment.

sections.heading: Step 1 — Cool the Burn
sections.body: Hold the burned area under cool (not cold) running water for 10 to 20 minutes. This stops the burning process and reduces pain significantly. Do not use ice, iced water, or any creams or buttery substances.
sections.warning: Never use ice directly on a burn. It can cause further tissue damage.
sections.image_description: Person holding burned hand under a running tap

sections.heading: Step 2 — Cover the Burn
sections.body: Cover the burned area loosely with a sterile non-stick dressing or clean cling film. Do not wrap it tightly. If cling film is unavailable, a clean plastic bag works for hand burns.
sections.warning: Do not use fluffy cotton or anything that can stick to the wound.
sections.image_description: Burned hand loosely wrapped in cling film

sections.heading: Step 3 — Seek Help
sections.body: Seek medical help for any burn larger than a postage stamp, burns on the face, hands, feet, genitals or joints, and all chemical or electrical burns. Burns in children under 5 or adults over 60 also need urgent care.
sections.warning: Do not pop blisters. They protect against infection.
sections.image_description: Diagram showing burn severity levels on skin

sections.heading: Step 4 — Manage Pain
sections.body: Give paracetamol or ibuprofen for pain if available and the person is not allergic. Keep the person warm as burns cause rapid heat loss. Offer fluids if the person is conscious and not vomiting.
sections.warning: Do not give aspirin to anyone under 16.

when_to_use: When someone has been burned by fire, hot liquid, steam, hot metal, or chemicals.
do_not: Use butter, toothpaste, or any cream
Remove clothing stuck to the burn
Use fluffy dressings that can stick
sources: British Red Cross First Aid Manual
